Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

There are many interesting elements to this manuscript.

The manuscripts explores the impact of interactions between two different entraining factors in circadian behaviours in the sea anemone, Nematostella. The authors view these interactions in terms of a framework called 'sensory conflict', which sets in motion a logical conflict in the way I view the results. I do not see why the 'sensory conflict' framework is required at all, and the fact all data are explored in such a rigid manner leads me to feel that the real interactions that may be important to Nematostella biology could well be lost. Another factor to consider is that there are many environmental cycles in the natural world in addition to the two explored here, including, but not limited to the lunar cycle, tides/currents, salinity, nutrition, UV/DNA damage, oxidation/reduction cycles… do they all cause conflicts? If they did, nothing would happen. Some may synergize or interact in an entire suite of different manners. The interaction would be the interesting element.

I am not sure you are looking at desynchronization at all. If both entraining signals have independent peaks, and you shift their alignments, you would have more peaks, e.g., more than one peak per 24 hours, one for light and one for temperature. Given the noise of the readout, two peaks may just look like noise/desynchronization. In fact, my explanation fits the data in 3A 12 hour offset quite well. You in fact recover a peak rapidly when going into constant darkness, so going back from two nonaligned inputs to one input, dark, which supports locomotory behaviour. I'd encourage you to think of the two entertainers shifting their alignments, and the consequences on your readout.

I'd argue that every statement that assumes the framework of 'sensory conflict' is a real thing in the animal and that the data show how this sensory conflict is impacted is not grammatically correct. I read the results carefully a number of times and thinking about the results simply as phase shifting does not in any way make the data more difficult to understand, and in fact makes it easier. If the phases of two different inputs were exactly aligned, for example temperature and light, they would still interact. If the phase of one were shifted so that the peak were now at a different point in a 24 hour cycle, they would still interact, presumably in a different manner. Is one conflict and the other not? In my mind they are just different examples, not one being a conflict and the other not a conflict.

L24. "Existing studies are limited in the range of tested zeitgeber relationships, and also in their taxonomic breadth, which is restricted to insects and vertebrates among animals. " This is clearly incorrect. There are in fact papers going back over a decade looking into many interacting entraining factors in the same cnidarian phylum, e.g., PMID: 31294494 and quite a volume of papers looking at interactions between two different light entrainers, daylight and moonlight, e.g., PMID: 17947585. There are also some very good papers on tide and light interactions in molluscs (PMCID: PMC3179051), season and temperature and tide (PMID: 33736335), lots on marine isopods, polychaete worms and I'm sure many, many others. PMID: 31294494 even looks at interactions between multiple entrainers, including temperature and light at the transcriptome level. These may not have applied the authors 'sensory conflict' framework, but they look at interactions between inputs, and seem more likely to be biologically relevant in my view. The authors do indeed have some interesting results and have done experiments not covered in the literature just mentioned, but they should look at their new results in light of these previous analyses.

Where the results in Figure 3 replicated? These are the core data that are the foundation of the manuscript. As the results do not align well with the authors' own previous constant temperature experiments, this replication would seem particularly important. I may have simply missed this somehow.

These two statements both occur in the legend to Figure 1: ZT0 refers to the coldest time point AND ZT0 always refers to lights-on. Which is true? Also, in this figure, what does the color coding of animals indicate?

The format of Figure 1B needs to be improved, which I simply do not understand. What was the feeding regimen of the animals, and could it impact the results? What was changed, and when, is not clear from the figure at all. The second part of Figure 1B does not make sense to me; I do not understand the concept of the schematic. Why do the periodograms flatline at midpoint through the light period in freerun? I suggest a major reconfiguration and more detail in the legend.

L183. I do not see the point of the masking effects discussion, though it would be fair to say I rarely do. Same with L434 and elsewhere.

Does the NORMA-Gene algorithm used for qPCR utilize control genes? None are mentioned. Without understanding the method used to control trusting the qPCR cycles isn't possible.

As discussed above, my major issue with the manuscript is the 'sensory conflict' focus that I believe makes the results very difficult to understand. Other reviewers may not share this view, but I think it devalues the excellent and interesting data in an unnecessary way.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

The study represents a large dataset of complex experiments designed to better understand the molecular response to sensory conflict in a basal metazoan. While the study reports a large number of intriguing results, the sheer volume of information makes it difficult to follow the results and discussion. This manuscript would benefit from additional streamlining that could help the flow and readability of the results. For example, the Discussion section of this manuscript is only three pages long, with no references back to individual figures or panels to help readers understand the authors' logic for the conclusions that have been drawn. In contrast, the Results section is roughly seven pages (not including figures) and much of it is extremely difficult to follow. This is particularly challenging given the large number of experiments and parameterizations that are utilized to explain the results. This discrepancy between results and discussion makes me wonder if all the results are indeed discussed, or if some may be better placed in supplemental information, allowing room for more in-depth discussion of the key results.

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Sensory conflict disrupts circadian rhythms in the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by Christian Rutz (Senior Editor) and a Reviewing Editor.

The manuscript has been improved significantly, Reviewer 2 however, raised some remaining aspects that we ask you to address, as they are particularly relevant for the chronobiological interpretation of your work.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors did an excellent job addressing my concerns and suggestions and I think the quality of the manuscript has improved considerably. I have only a few minor remarks listed below. My main concern that temperature cycles cannot by themselves entrain the Nematostella circadian clock has been addressed by an additional frequency demultiplication experiment. The results of this experiment are convincing: Animals kept in 6h : 6h temperature cycles display a main rhythmic component with a ~25 h period, showing that the rhythm is not simply driven by temperature. Since the animals also show no free-running circadian rhythms after temperature entrainment, it can also be ruled out that the observed 25 h period simply reflects free-running behaviour one would expect under constant conditions. Nevertheless, I still don't think it is fair to say that temperature cycles entrain the circadian clock of Nematostella. In my view the authors show that temperature cycles clearly influence or modulate the clock, but they do not entrain it. By definition, true entrainment must fulfil two criteria. First, the period of the observed rhythm must equal the period of the entraining cycle (here the temperature cycle) and establish a stable phase relationship to each other. Second, after release into constant conditions, the observed rhythm must continue with the same phase established during the entrainment cycle (e.g., Dunlap et al. 2004; Chronobiology: Biological Timekeeping, Sinauer Associates). None of these criteria are fulfilled (1: no stable phase relationship-the animals fall into two groups, and 2: no rhythm observed in free running conditions after the entrainment cycle), and there are also no molecular rhythms observed in any of the clock genes after temperature cycles. For these reasons I think the authors need to tone down their claim that temperature cycles entrain the Nematostella circadian clock. On the other hand, I think the sensory conflict experiments convincingly show that temperature cycles do influence behaviour and molecular rhythms in combined LD and TC conditions, but again this only demonstrates that temperature cycles influence or modulate the circadian clock. The text should be changed accordingly to reflect these differences.

results.result: Temperature cycles drive rhythmic locomotor behavior in Nematostella vectensis. Anemones exposed to environmentally realistic temperature cycles (14-26°C or 8-32°C) in constant darkness exhibited rhythmic behavior with peak activity at ZT18 (where ZT0 is the coldest point). Only the cryptochrome gene Cry2 showed rhythmic expression during temperature cycles, with peak expression at ZT0, while no clock genes were rhythmic during free-run.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C57-C59, C72-C73, C76-C80 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 2a) showing rhythmic locomotor activity during temperature cycles and qRT-PCR data (Figure 2c) showing Cry2 rhythmicity. The temperature ranges used are within natural variation experienced by the source population (C77). Statistical tests confirm rhythmicity (LSP p<0.001, eJTK p<0.001).

results.result: Sensory conflict between light and temperature cycles disrupts circadian behavior in Nematostella, with effects on both entrained and free-running rhythms. Aligned cycles (lights-on at coldest temperature) produced robust rhythmic behavior during entrainment and free-run. Large misalignments (10-12 hr offsets) severely disrupted rhythmic behavior, reduced synchronization among individuals, and altered free-running rhythms, demonstrating effects on the endogenous clock rather than simple masking. Smaller offsets (0-8 hr) maintained relatively normal rhythmic behavior, though Off6 showed a phase delay.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C60-C127 are comprehensively supported by behavioral data across multiple offset conditions (Figure 3, Tables 1-2). Statistical tests confirm disruption at large offsets (eJTK, LSP, Rayleigh tests, LMM, CircaCompare) and maintenance of rhythmicity at smaller offsets. Clustering analysis (Figure 4) validates the grouping of normal vs. disrupted conditions. Free-running data demonstrate endogenous clock disruption rather than masking effects. The non-linear relationship between offset and disruption is well-documented.

results.result: Sensory conflict substantially alters diel gene expression patterns in Nematostella. Under aligned conditions, 1009 genes were differentially expressed between light and dark, while 627 genes were DE during SC. The 277 genes DE in both conditions showed a negative correlation (r=-0.59) in log-fold changes, indicating inversion of expression patterns. Temperature was a stronger regulator than light (1978 vs. 25 genes), and temperature-responsive genes were enriched for transcription factor binding and oxidoreductase activity. Motif analysis revealed enrichment of bZIP binding sites in genes affected by SC.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C63-C64, C135-C159 are supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis (limma-voom) with appropriate statistical methods. DAPC analysis (Figure 5a) confirms the inversion of gene expression patterns. The negative correlation between aligned and SC conditions is statistically significant. GO enrichment and motif analysis (HOMER) provide functional context. Sample sizes (3 biological replicates per time point) and statistical thresholds (p<0.05 with FDR correction) are appropriate.

results.result: Many genes maintained or gained rhythmicity during sensory conflict, with temperature-responsive genes showing robust rhythmic expression. Under aligned conditions, 2868 genes were rhythmic (18% of transcriptome), while 2440 genes were rhythmic during SC, with 1116 shared. 1225 genes lost rhythmicity (Align-specific) and 921 gained rhythmicity (SC-specific). The vast majority of shared rhythmic genes (98%) shifted phase by a median of 10.3 hr, tracking the temperature cycle. 647 genes closely followed temperature phase and were enriched for transcription factor activity and metabolic terms. Amplitudes of shared rhythmic genes were modestly reduced (7.1%) during SC.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12, C67, C161-C192 are supported by RAIN rhythmicity analysis (p<0.01) with validation from ECHO and DryR showing strong agreement. Phase analysis using CircaCompare demonstrates the phase shifts. The identification of temperature-tracking genes (647 genes with 10-12 hr phase shift relative to light but no shift relative to temperature) is methodologically sound. GO enrichment analysis provides functional context. Statistical comparisons of amplitude and expression levels use appropriate tests (Wilcoxon). The bimodal phase distributions are confirmed by Rayleigh tests.

results.result: Sensory conflict disrupts co-expressed gene modules related to cellular metabolism and weakens correlations between rhythmic genes. WGCNA analysis revealed that intramodular connectivity (kIM) was reduced by 23% during SC, and total network connectivity (kTotal) was reduced by 12%. The correlation between genes and their module eigengenes (kME) decreased by 5.6%, and the variance explained by eigengenes (propVar) decreased by 8.2%. Sliding window enrichment analysis showed dramatic changes to metabolic gene expression timing, with most enriched terms in aligned conditions losing enrichment during SC. Half of module eigengenes (7/14) remained rhythmic and shifted 10-12 hr with temperature.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66, C168-C175, C197-C205, C215 are supported by WGCNA analysis with appropriate parameters (soft-thresholding power, signed hybrid adjacency, bicor correlation). Statistical comparisons of connectivity metrics use Wilcoxon tests with highly significant p-values (p<1×10^-15). Sliding window enrichment analysis (GO_MWU, clusterProfiler) with 4-hr windows provides temporal resolution of functional changes. Module eigengene rhythmicity is confirmed by LSP tests (p<0.01). The functional enrichment results (Figure 5e, Figure 6) are consistent with metabolic disruption.

results.result: Light and temperature interact to set the phase of Nematostella's circadian clock, with neither cue dominating. Phase analysis showed that Off4-cycle and Off8-cycle groups were significantly closer to light-entrained phases (Wilcoxon p<0.05), while other groups were approximately equidistant between light and temperature zeitgebers. Free-running phases showed no evidence of being primarily determined by either light or temperature. This demonstrates that both cues contribute to clock entrainment, and normal rhythmic behavior is only possible under certain environmental relationships.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C69, C131-C134, C209-C210 are supported by phase relationship analysis (Figure 3d) comparing observed phases to expected light-entrained and temperature-entrained phases. Statistical tests (paired Wilcoxon rank tests) confirm the closer alignment to light for specific groups. The conclusion that neither cue dominates is supported by the disruption observed at large offsets rather than simple following of one zeitgeber. However, the caveat about lower statistical power for free-running groups (C133) is appropriately noted.

results.result: Despite behavioral disruption, some rhythmic metabolic processes persist during sensory conflict. Many genes remained rhythmic and in-phase with temperature, and other genes gained rhythmicity. Genes related to autophagy and endocytosis shifted phase following temperature, while genes related to ribosome and protein metabolism lost rhythmicity. A substantial portion of the transcriptome (7%) remained rhythmic even during conditions that severely disrupted behavior. These changes likely have bioenergetic consequences, as circadian clocks regulate metabolic homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C216-C218, C279, C290-C295 are supported by RNA-seq data showing continued rhythmicity during SC (2440 rhythmic genes) and enrichment analysis identifying functional categories (Figure 5e). The observation that 921 genes gained rhythmicity (SC-specific) demonstrates persistence of some rhythmic processes. The inference about bioenergetic consequences (C295) is reasonable given established knowledge about clock function in metabolism (supported by citations), though direct physiological measurements are not provided in this study.

results.result: Core clock gene expression patterns suggest differential regulation by light and temperature. Cry2 expression was driven by both light and temperature cycles, supporting its role in the core clock, while Cry1a and Cry1b expression appears driven only by light, suggesting photosensor roles. Other putative clock genes (Helt, CIPC, PAR-bZIP-a, PAR-bZIP-c) were strongly rhythmic in both aligned and SC conditions. During SC, CIPC, Cry2, and PAR-bZIP-c advanced in phase by 5-8 hr, while Clock, Helt, and PAR-bZIP-a remained in-phase with light, suggesting light controls rhythmic expression of some core clock components.
results.evaluation: Claims C258-C266 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 2c) and RNA-seq data (Figure 5d, Table 3). The differential response of cryptochromes to light vs. temperature is clearly demonstrated. Phase analysis using CircaCompare shows the differential phase shifts of clock genes during SC. The inference about Cry2's core clock role vs. Cry1a/b photosensor roles (C258-C259) is reasonable based on expression patterns and supported by citation to Reitzel et al. 2013. However, functional validation (e.g., knockdown experiments) is not provided.

results.result: Clock mRNA did not oscillate during temperature cycles and was one of only 24 genes to directly follow the light cycle. Together with evidence that Clock expression is induced by blue light, this suggests rhythmic Clock expression is entirely blue light-driven and may not be required for rhythmic behavior. This unusual pattern may suggest that temperature cycles do not entrain circadian rhythms in Nematostella in the same way as light.
results.evaluation: Claims C267-C269, C273 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 2c) showing no Clock oscillation during temperature cycles and RNA-seq data identifying Clock among the 24 genes following light. The inference about blue light-driven expression (C269) combines current data with citation to Leach and Reitzel 2020. However, the speculation that this means temperature doesn't entrain rhythms "in the same way" (C273) is not well-supported, as behavioral data clearly show temperature effects. The claim that rhythmic Clock expression is "not required for rhythmic behavior" (C269) is speculative without functional validation. The authors appropriately note this would be unusual compared to other systems (C270-C272).

results.result: Comparison with a previous study (Oren et al. 2015) shows that core clock gene phases are within 4 hr between studies (except Cry1b), but there is little overlap in rhythmic genes overall (only 32% of genes rhythmic in Oren et al. 2015 had p<0.05 in current study). Core clock gene expression was not altered by adding a temperature cycle in-phase with light.
results.evaluation: Claims C193-C196 are supported by re-analysis of Oren et al. 2015 data and comparison with current study (Table 3). The phase comparison is quantitative and shows good agreement for core clock genes. The low overlap in rhythmic genes (C194) is clearly documented. The speculation about reasons for differences (C195) is appropriately cautious. The conclusion about temperature not altering core clock gene expression when in-phase with light (C196) is reasonable based on the phase comparisons, though this is an inference from comparing two studies rather than a direct experimental test.

results.result: Behavioral patterns during entrainment differed from free-running patterns, indicating complex interactions between direct effects and endogenous rhythms. During 6 hr offset, endogenous rhythms were disrupted but entrainment behavior was normal (light and temperature directly drove behavior). During 12 hr offset, endogenous rhythms were relatively robust but entrainment behavior was arrhythmic (misaligned cycles masked endogenous rhythms). Non-linear dynamics were observed, with phase differences as small as 2 hr producing different outcomes. Free-running rhythms were most disrupted at 6 hr and 10 hr offsets but robust at 4 hr and 8 hr offsets.
results.evaluation: Claims C223-C227, C231-C234 are supported by comparison of entrainment and free-running data (Figure 3, Tables 1-2). The contrasting patterns at 6 hr (Off6-FR arrhythmic, Off6-cycle rhythmic) and 12 hr (Off12-FR rhythmic, Off12-cycle arrhythmic) are clearly documented. The inference about masking vs. direct driving (C225, C227) is reasonable given the data patterns. The non-linear dynamics (C232) are evident from the non-monotonic relationship between offset and disruption. The comparison to Drosophila central clock behavior (C231) is appropriate given the similar pattern of disruption rather than following a single zeitgeber.

results.result: Motif analysis suggests bZIP and possibly SOX family transcription factors regulate circadian gene expression in Nematostella. There was strong agreement between three rhythmicity detection methods (RAIN, ECHO, DryR). Promoters of shared rhythmic genes were enriched for bZIP binding sites (p=1×10^-6). PAR-bZIP and SOX proteins regulate circadian outputs in bilaterians, and Nematostella PAR-bZIP and SOX genes were robustly rhythmic during both aligned and SC conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C160, C255-C257 are supported by motif enrichment analysis using HOMER (Figure 5—source data 3) with appropriate statistical thresholds (p<1×10^-5 for known motifs). The agreement between rhythmicity detection methods (C160) validates the analytical approach. The enrichment of bZIP motifs in shared rhythmic genes is statistically significant. The connection to bilaterian clock regulation (C256) is supported by citations. The observation that PAR-bZIP and SOX genes are rhythmic (C257) is from RNA-seq data. However, the inference that these factors "regulate" circadian expression (C255) is based on motif enrichment and comparative biology rather than direct functional evidence.

results.result: The study demonstrates for the first time that diel temperature cycles influence circadian rhythms in a cnidarian, with broad effects on gene expression and behavior. The disruptive effects were chronic changes after weeks of acclimation, not acute responses. However, temperature may not be a true zeitgeber since free-running rhythms were weak and free-running molecular rhythms in core clock genes were not observed. This weakness may not be surprising given that cnidarian rhythms are generally weaker than bilaterian rhythms. The data provide strong but not definitive evidence for temperature entrainment.
results.evaluation: Claims C211, C306-C312 appropriately characterize the study's contribution and limitations. The chronic nature of effects (C211) is supported by the experimental design (≥2 weeks acclimation). The novelty claim (C311) appears accurate based on literature review (C56). The cautious conclusion about temperature as a zeitgeber (C306, C312) is appropriate given the weak free-running rhythms and lack of free-running molecular rhythms in core clock genes. The contextualization with general cnidarian rhythm characteristics (C307-C308) is supported by citations. The suggestion for future work (C310) is reasonable. The overall assessment as "strong but not definitive" evidence (C312) is a fair characterization.

results.result: There are limits to the clock's ability to integrate conflicting sensory information, but there is also surprising robustness of behavioral and transcriptional rhythmicity. Normal organismal rhythms are only possible under certain environmental conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16, C70 are supported by the comprehensive behavioral and transcriptional data. Limits are demonstrated by disruption at large offsets (C15, Figure 3), while robustness is shown by maintained rhythmicity at smaller offsets and continued rhythmic gene expression during SC (C16, Figures 3, 5). The conclusion that normal rhythms require certain environmental relationships (C70) follows logically from the observation that large misalignments disrupt behavior. These are appropriate summary statements of the main findings.

results.result: Background and motivation claims establish the context for studying sensory conflict in circadian biology. These include established knowledge about circadian clocks, zeitgebers, sensory conflict, and the importance of cnidarian models. The claims identify gaps in knowledge regarding multi-zeitgeber systems and transcriptional responses to sensory conflict.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C56 are background and motivation statements supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These claims accurately represent the state of knowledge in circadian biology and identify legitimate research gaps. The phylogenetic relationship of Cnidaria to Bilateria (C43) is supported by citation. The ecological context for Nematostella (C52-C54) is supported by citations. The statement that no studies have investigated thermal entrainment in non-bilaterians (C56) appears accurate based on the literature review. These claims provide appropriate context but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Discussion claims interpret the findings in broader context, compare with other systems (especially Drosophila), speculate about mechanisms, and discuss implications. These include comparisons to bilaterian clock organization, speculation about cellular mechanisms, discussion of ecological context, and suggestions for future work.
results.evaluation: Claims C206-C305 are primarily discussion and interpretation. Many are appropriately supported by the data and citations (e.g., comparisons to Drosophila C228-C230, ecological context C300-C303). However, several involve speculation about mechanisms without direct evidence (e.g., C240-C241 about neuronal organization, C246-C249 about single vs. multiple clocks, C274-C275 about Clock function, C280 about functional significance of SC-specific genes, C304-C305 about adaptive significance). The speculation is generally appropriate and clearly identified as such, but these claims cannot be evaluated as definitively supported or unsupported. The suggestions for future work (C250, C299, C310) are reasonable but not testable results. The novelty claim (C278) appears accurate.
